title: ÆTHER: Storm Entry (hero entry BGM)
story: Night of a temple festival. A storm breaks, the crowd scatters, and through the rain one man walks in: the hero's first appearance in the film.

brief.notes: Jithesh 30 Oct 07:49: 'without my help, create one or two interesting, fascinating hero entry BGMs, a proper cinematic main BGM of the movie.' Made autonomously from every rule so far: section 8 refs (mid-tempo menace, 112 BPM, dark minor with chromatic bends, synth bass + processed hits, wordless crowd chants, loud), 9.1-9.3 Broken Heritage, 3-note motif at both ends, reversed veena swell ONCE (the reveal), 9.9 the scene's own sounds as instruments (thunder = the boom, rain on a tin roof = the hi-hat, a temple bell, an iron chain dragged = a percussive scrape), 9.10 composed transitions, 9.11 a new hook every 8-12 s, 9.12 mystery start with two sounds and about half real instruments, 9.13 earworm riff + grab in 3 s + wow moments (one-beat silence and slam, nadaswaram-vs-synth duel that speeds up, whole-step key lift), 9.14-9.15 raga melody with gamakam written in South Indian film style, 9.16 natural dry nadaswaram/thavil/violin. Different from The Return (dark city walk) and Neon Raja (cyberpunk). Prompt mode (music_v2).

prompt: A brand-new mass hero ENTRY theme written the way today's biggest Tamil and Telugu film composers score the hero's first appearance: goosebumps, swagger, a crowd-roaring theatre moment. The scene: a temple festival at night, a storm breaks, and the hero walks in through the rain. No lyrics, no singer; deep wordless male crowd chants and shouts ('hey!', 'ho!') answer the hook. About 112 BPM felt as a heavy half-time swagger, dark minor raga with a sharp fourth (like Shanmukhapriya) and chromatic semitone bends: menacing and proud. INDIAN TOUCH IN THE WRITING: a whistle-able 5-note hero hook phrased like a singer, with fast Carnatic gamakam turns, slides and bent held notes on every lead, the Tamil mass bounce, tight unison stabs with the melody, call and response, the hook coming back bigger each time, a korvai-style ending (a rhythmic phrase played three times landing on the final hit). Balance: real instruments (nadaswaram, thavil, violins, low brass, mridangam) carry half the music, played close, natural and dry like real musicians, no echo on them; the other half is fresh electronics: a thick dark synth bass, a gritty bent synth lead, and the storm's own sounds turned into instruments: a thunder crack is the giant boom, rain on a tin roof is the hi-hat, an iron chain dragged on stone is a scraping percussion hit, a temple bell rings on the downbeats; a mridangam pitched down and stretched becomes the deep bass hit. Timeline: 0-3 s: a huge thunder crack with a deep cinematic boom, then only two sounds: rain on the tin roof ticking a slow pulse and a gritty synth lead playing a rising 3-note call (root, minor third, fifth, last note bent upward). 3-10 s: mystery: the synth bass creeps in under the rain pulse, one temple bell, the hero hook hinted on a low bent synth, the crowd breathing a low hum. 10-12 s: one reversed veena swell rising into a massive full-band hit and a crowd 'HEY!'. 12-22 s: the swagger groove slams in: heavy drums, thick synth bass, the chain scrape on every bar, the 5-note hook on the gritty synth lead, crowd chants answering every phrase. 22-32 s: the hook moves to a loud, natural nadaswaram over the thavil playing the mass bounce, low brass stabs in unison with the melody, violins add a climbing counter-melody. 32-42 s: a duel: the nadaswaram and the synth lead trade the hook, phrases getting shorter and faster, the thavil doubles time, the melodic bass moving under them like a second melody. 42-43 s: the whole band stops dead for one beat, only the rain. 43-55 s: BANG, the biggest slam: the hook lifted up a whole step, full brass, violins in Indian-style unison, crowd chant on every accent, thunder booms on the downbeats, never thinning out. 55-68 s: the triumphant walk: a new variation of the hook on violins and nadaswaram together, the synth lead bending above, drums at full power, a thavil roll building. 68-75 s: the ending: a rhythmic korvai phrase played three times by the whole band, landing on one huge final hit with a thunder crack and sub drop, then the lone 3-note call bends and rings out over the rain. Very loud, punchy, clean, dark, low-mid heavy, wide cinematic mix. Not Western trailer music, not Hollywood, not EDM, no side-chain pumping, no white-noise risers, no filter sweeps, no long quiet stretches, no wall of synths, no lyrics.
